summary: A 1970 proposed user-user protocol by G. H. Mealy.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 91 proposes a protocol above the Host-Host layer for user processes to exchange records, control information, and status. It uses flags to identify the type and size of following data.

questions: what is a logical record in the arpanet
what is the proposed user-user protocol
subtitle: A proposal for tagging data and control information exchanged between user processes.

tldr.problem: The lower-level IMP-IMP and Host-Host protocols do not let user processes agree on data representation or verify that a requested action was completed.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal precedes data blocks with a four-bit operation flag and, when needed, a count field that gives the block length.
tldr.outcome: RFC 91 is a proposed user-user protocol and a sketch of a PDP-10 implementation, not a settled standard.

today: RFC 91 is a proposed user-user protocol. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

sections.title: A Protocol Between User Processes
sections.content:
George Mealy proposes making network communication look like input and output to user programs. He wants the protocol to support logical records, allow existing programs to access remote files where possible, and be implementable through host system calls.

The proposal addresses two issues left to this level: processes on different hosts may need local agreements about data representation, and the lower-level protocols do not confirm that a requested user action was completed.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal gives user programs a way to label data and request actions from other programs. It leaves data-format choices to local agreement between the processes.

sections.title: Flags, Counts, and Records
sections.content:
The data on a link is a sequence of flags followed by possible data blocks, in the form OPERATION, COUNT, DATA. The OPERATION field is always 4 bits. When present, the COUNT field gives the number of following data bytes; it is 8 bits except in EOM, where it is 16 bits.

The flags identify record, group, and file separators; byte size; control and status data; labels; keys; ASCII; and blocks. A SIZE flag must occur in each message before a block flag, except ASCII. The EOM flag marks the end of useful message data and repeats the total bit count as an error check.
sections.plainLanguage: Each data block can have a flag saying what it contains and how much follows. Other flags mark records, groups, files, and the end of a message.

sections.title: Control and Status Exchange
sections.content:
The CONTROL flag carries a request for an action, while STATUS carries information about the result. Their data meanings are left to local agreement between the user processes. A LABEL can identify data, and KEY can identify a record, data item, or storage block.

The SYS flag is intended for data interpreted by the receiving host system rather than an ordinary user process. The RFC connects this idea to unresolved questions about logging in to a remote host.
sections.plainLanguage: Processes can send control requests and return status, but they must agree locally on what the attached data means. SYS is a proposed way to send information directly to the receiving host.

sections.title: The PDP-10 Implementation Sketch
sections.content:
Mealy outlines five PDP-10 operations: PUTF to send a flag, PUTD to send data, PUT to send a record, GETFD to receive a flag or data, and GET to receive a record. The first implementation is planned as user routines, though the RFC describes monitor calls.

The file-transfer example uses CONTROL and LABEL data to open a file, requests records, receives STATUS and data, and later requests a close. The author estimates the implementation at about 400 instructions and leaves logon and interrupt handling as questions for further thought.
sections.plainLanguage: The implementation sketch provides operations for sending flags and data and for receiving records. The RFC presents it as one host-specific example, not a finished general implementation.
